data.title: Callus (callosity) — viva
data.summary: Disorders of keratinisation · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Callus (callosity)** (Disorders of keratinisation)_

**Q1. What is a callus?**
- Diffuse, plaque-like, yellowish thickening of the stratum corneum (hyperkeratosis) at sites of repeated friction or intermittent pressure, without a central core; protective response
- Occupational calluses ('occupational stigmata'): tailor's (fingers), guitarist's fingertips, prayer callus (forehead/knees — 'prayer nodules'), tennis player's palm, writer's callus, cobbler's, farmer's palms; Russell's sign (knuckle calluses from self-induced vomiting in bulimia)

**Q2. Pathogenesis.**
- Repeated friction/pressure → increased keratinocyte proliferation and retention hyperkeratosis to protect underlying tissue
- Predisposing: ill-fitting footwear, high heels, foot deformities (hallux valgus, flat/high-arched feet), abnormal gait, obesity, peripheral neuropathy (diabetes, leprosy — calluses precede neuropathic ulcers), barefoot walking

**Q3. Differentiate callus, corn and plantar wart.**
- Callus: broad diffuse thickening over pressure/friction areas, skin lines preserved, little pain, no core
- Corn: circumscribed with central translucent conical core pointing inwards, painful on direct pressure, skin lines pass through
- Wart: interrupts skin lines, black dots (thrombosed capillaries) on paring, painful on lateral squeeze

**Q4. Why are calluses important in diabetes and leprosy?**
- In insensate feet, callus acts like a foreign body increasing plantar pressure → haemorrhage beneath callus → neuropathic ulcer; regular callus debridement and offloading footwear (MCR) prevent ulceration

**Q5. Management.**
- Remove cause: proper well-fitting footwear, padding, insoles/orthotics, correct foot deformity, offloading
- Paring with a scalpel or pumice stone after soaking
- Keratolytics: salicylic acid 10–40% (plasters/ointments), urea 20–40%, lactic acid; emollients
- Avoid aggressive self-treatment in diabetics; podiatry referral

**Q6. Histopathology of a callus.**
- Compact orthohyperkeratosis without parakeratosis plug, thickened granular layer may be thin, mild acanthosis; no viral cytopathic changes (vs wart); dermis may show fibrosis

**Q7. What occupational calluses are known?**
- Occupational marks: guitar/violin players' fingertips, tailor's/cobbler's calluses, prayer nodules (knees, forehead — 'prayer mark' in Muslims), 'surfer's knots', writer's callus on middle finger, sitting calluses (ischial — Indian squatting), Russell's sign (knuckle calluses from self-induced vomiting — bulimia)

**Q8. How do you assess the foot biomechanics?**
- Examine footwear and gait, pressure points, foot deformities (hallux valgus, hammer toes, pes cavus), podoscope/pedobarography; refer to podiatrist/orthotist for offloading insoles

**Q9. Complications in insensate feet.**
- Callus acts like a stone in the shoe — haemorrhage beneath the callus (pre-ulcerative sign) → neuropathic (mal perforans) ulcer, infection, osteomyelitis; routine paring and protective MCR footwear are preventive

**Q10. Describe the process of keratinisation and the cornified envelope (PYQ).**
- Basal keratinocytes (K5/K14) divide and move up: spinous (K1/K10, desmosomes), granular (keratohyaline granules — profilaggrin, loricrin; lamellar bodies — lipids), cornified layer (flattened anucleate corneocytes)
- Cornified envelope: cross-linked proteins (involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich proteins) by transglutaminases (TGM1, TGM3, TGM5) with covalently bound lipid envelope (ceramides); intercellular lipid lamellae (ceramides, cholesterol, FFA) — 'bricks and mortar' barrier
- Desquamation via kallikreins (KLK5/7) degrading corneodesmosomes, regulated by LEKTI (SPINK5)

**Q11. What keratolytics are used and how do they work?**
- Salicylic acid 10–40% (plasters/ ointment — dissolves intercellular cement), urea 20–40% (humectant and keratolytic at high strength), lactic acid 12%, propylene glycol; caution in diabetics/ neuropathy (chemical burns)

**Q12. What is the paring technique and safety?**
- Soften by soaking 10 min, pare with scalpel blade (no. 15) parallel to skin until pink skin appears, avoid drawing blood; in diabetics and leprosy patients refer to trained podiatry; pumice stone home maintenance

**Q13. Callus vs plantar wart vs corn on dermoscopy.**
- Callus: homogeneous yellowish structureless keratin with preserved dermatoglyphics
- Wart: interrupted dermatoglyphics, red-black dots (thrombosed capillaries)
- Corn: central translucent keratin core with surrounding callus, dermatoglyphics preserved around

**Q14. Callus in leprosy patients — prevention programme.**
- Daily self-care: soak feet 20 min, scrape with pumice, apply oil/ petroleum jelly, inspect for cracks, protective footwear (MCR/ microcellular rubber insoles), regular follow-up at disability prevention clinics

**Q15. What is the 'pre-ulcerative callus'?**
- Callus with underlying haemorrhage (dark discolouration) or blister — signals high pressure and impending ulcer in neuropathic feet; urgent offloading and debridement

## Quick spotter facts
- Diffuse yellow plaque over pressure point without core — callus
- Calluses in insensate foot precede neuropathic ulcers

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Mechanical and physical injuries; keratoderma). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
